Well, we are just shifting from one form of shitty journalism to another.

Journalism, real journalism, requires rigor. Sort of like science, there are rules and guidelines you should follow to help prevent you from bias and mistakes. Real (honest) journalists follow these kind of rules. Shitty big media, 24 hour news, youtube activists, and amateur bloggers don't (normally).

So you have to be careful to not jump from one shitty service to another just because its not as "mainstream", that goes double if you find yourself liking everything the source is saying, triple if your political views match.

I feel like news in a conflict. As you mentioned real journalism requires time. Take for instance the shooting in Charleston 20 years ago up here in Canada I would read about that 1-5 days later. A newspaper would have time to do fact checking and find out information from sources. Then it would be written, edited, and written again yielding the final piece.

This goes completely against the 'first to the story' that we like so much today. There are a few publications still doing old style news (such as the Economist) but they are all moving to complete subscription models as they can't generate the click-bait of CNN, Fox, MSNBC, etc.

Right, somewhere along the way it became more important to be "FIRSTLOL!" than to be accurate and thorough.

I've sometimes wondered if it would work out to make a news program that was "Last". Sort of like John Oliver's show. Where you come in a week later and sum up what happened, where things went wrong, what possible longer term implications there are. Make it more of a big picture and less of a race to mediocrity.

It's kind of hard to tell. It seems like for every honest journalist, who actually works to seek out and report truth, there are four or five others who will bend over backward to pump out superficial stories or, even worse, publish 'sponsored' content. My best advice would be don't judge a journalist by his or her publisher. Just because they are indie doesn't make them any less corrupt. It pains me to say that about my coworkers, but the reality is that there are many who are just out for the money.
yeah, I agree with the other comments here. I don't think we're in a journalism renaissance, but we're in dire need of one.

However, sadly, while the access is there I think the majority of people still rely on traditional news organisations and media in order to access news, and so don't see all these new sources, mainly because it's easier to listen to a guy on the telly tell you his opinion on what happened and let him select and tell you his own choice of sources, rather than go out there yourself and find out what is really going on.
